title: Research Explained #28 — How Would We Detect an Artificial Change in Spacetime?
html:
Suppose you switch on a device and a nearby atomic clock appears to tick differently. The shift returns every time the device turns on. The observation can be real while the explanation is still open. Did the device heat the clock, disturb a magnetic field or shake an optical component? The reference clock or the link that compares the two clocks could also have shifted. Each possibility predicts a different response when you change how the experiment is set up.

There is one more possibility to account for. If the device moves a heavy component, the component’s ordinary gravity changes at the sensor. Under general relativity, relocating a mass also changes the local tidal curvature predicted around it. A movable mass gives us a way to test what a detector should see from a known source before looking for an unfamiliar effect. Carroll, chapters 3–4

What each instrument measures

An ideal clock accumulates proper time, the elapsed time it records along its own path. Comparing two clocks tells us how their rates or elapsed times differ. A supported accelerometer senses the acceleration supplied by its support or by other nongravitational forces. In ideal free fall, it reads zero even in a curved spacetime. A pair of nearby freely falling probes can reveal a different quantity through their relative acceleration. That is a tidal measurement. Carroll, chapters 3–4

In a weak, slowly changing gravitational environment, it helps to think of the gravitational potential as a landscape. Two clocks can compare the heights of two points on that landscape. The slope tells you how an object released from rest initially accelerates relative to a stationary lab. When two nearby objects sit on different slopes, their free-fall accelerations differ. That change in slope is the weak-field picture of a tidal effect.

Imagine an accelerating cabin in otherwise flat spacetime. A sensor bolted to the wall feels the cabin push it, and clocks held at opposite ends along the direction of acceleration can tick at different rates. Release two probes at the same instant in a common inertial frame in which both are initially at rest. Their separation stays constant in that frame. Near a gravitating mass their separation can change in free fall. The cabin example shows why a clock or acceleration reading alone leaves the tidal question open. Carroll, chapters 3–4

Einstein’s field equation connects spacetime geometry to its sources.

\[ G_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}=\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}T_{\mu\nu}. \]

Here \(G_{\mu\nu}\) is the Einstein tensor, \(g_{\mu\nu}\) is the metric, \(\Lambda\) is the cosmological constant, \(G\) is Newton’s gravitational constant, \(c\) is the speed of light and \(T_{\mu\nu}\) describes stress and energy. To test a specific source, we need a model connecting the geometry it produces to the clock readings, optical signals or test-mass trajectories we can actually record. Carroll, chapter 4

Clocks compare rates

For two identical stationary clocks A and B in a common static weak field, the leading gravitational contribution to the compared fractional rate difference is

\[ \frac{f_B-f_A}{f_A}\simeq\frac{\Phi_B-\Phi_A}{c^2}. \]

The clock at higher potential runs faster in this comparison. The equation gives the gravitational contribution after accounting for motion and shifts in the clocks and their comparison link. For clocks at different elevations near Earth, a millimetre of vertical separation corresponds to a fractional difference of about \(1.1\times10^{-19}\). Carroll, chapter 4 · Bothwell et al., Eq. 1

In 2022, Tobias Bothwell and colleagues resolved a frequency gradient consistent with Earth’s gravitational redshift inside one millimetre-scale sample of ultracold strontium-87. The spatial mapping yielded a gradient of \(-9.8(2.3)\times10^{-20}\) per millimetre after accounting for differential systematics, with the sign set by their coordinate direction. The team also compared two regions of the sample synchronously for 92 hours and reached a fractional statistical precision of \(7.6\times10^{-21}\). The first number describes the measured slope and its uncertainty. The second describes the statistical precision of the regional comparison. Bothwell et al., Figs. 3–4 and Table 1

Atom interferometers compare motion with a laser reference

Laser pulses can split and recombine atomic matter waves. The last pulse converts the phase difference into a change in how many atoms end up in each measured state. In a common three-pulse configuration, that phase helps infer how the atoms accelerate relative to the laser phase reference. For ideal short pulses at \(0,T,2T\), the leading acceleration contribution is \(\mathbf{k}_{\rm eff}\cdot\mathbf{a}_{\rm rel}T^2\). Here \(\mathbf{k}_{\rm eff}\) is the effective laser wave vector in inverse metres, \(\mathbf{a}_{\rm rel}\) is the constant relative acceleration in metres per second squared, and \(T\) is the pulse spacing in seconds. The laser frequency sweep and programmed phases also enter the readout. Rotation, vibration and gravity gradients matter in a real instrument. Mark Kasevich and Steven Chu demonstrated this type of Raman atom interferometry in 1991. Kasevich and Chu, pp. 181–182

In 2007, Jeffrey Fixler and colleagues repositioned a lead source whose mass and geometry they had measured and measured the change in differential acceleration between two vertically separated samples of cesium atoms. They fitted the response with a Newtonian source model to infer \(G\). The experiment shows how a known change in source position can give a measurable, predictable signal. In a separate study, Achim Peters and colleagues compared an atom gravimeter with a falling-glass Michelson gravimeter at the same laboratory site and reported agreement within seven parts in a billion. Fixler et al. · Fixler’s apparatus and analysis · Peters et al., journal abstract

LIGO measures a different kind of signal

On September 14, 2015, LIGO’s Hanford and Livingston detectors registered a transient signal consistent with a merger of two black holes. The reported peak gravitational-wave strain was about \(10^{-21}\). Strain is dimensionless. For equal arms and a long-wavelength, plus-polarized wave arriving perpendicular to their plane with its polarization axes aligned to the arms, strain equals the change in the difference between their lengths divided by the unperturbed arm length. The actual readout is calibrated and depends on the detector’s response to the wave’s orientation, polarization and frequency. Discovery paper, abstract and Fig. 1 · Calibration paper

The two sites’ timing, waveform and noise analysis helped establish the detection. The peak strain describes that event. A near-static laboratory source calls for a measurement model and sensitivity estimate suited to its own spatial pattern and modulation frequency. Discovery paper · Calibration paper

What would an ordinary movable mass produce?

Take a spherically symmetric source of \(1{,}000\) kilograms with a radius strictly less than one metre. At a test point one metre from its centre and outside the mass, Newtonian gravity predicts an inward acceleration of \(GM/r^2\), or \(6.67\times10^{-8}\) metres per second squared, using \(G=6.67430\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\) and \(c=299{,}792{,}458\,\mathrm{m/s}\) for the clock calculation below. That is about \(6.8\times10^{-9}\) times standard gravity. Carroll, chapter 4 · NIST CODATA constants

Now put ideal stationary clocks one and two metres from the centre. The source’s contribution to the potential is \(-GM/r\). The outer clock is higher in potential by \(GM(1/r_1-1/r_2)\), about \(3.34\times10^{-8}\) square metres per second squared. Dividing by \(c^2\) gives a fractional rate difference of about \(3.7\times10^{-25}\). These are analytic estimates of the source contribution. For an actual two-position experiment we would calculate each observable in both source positions, then subtract. A mass that shifts only slightly can give a much smaller difference between states than its full field at one position. Supports, counterweights and other moving hardware contribute their own ordinary gravity. Earth’s background field and the detector response also enter the analysis. Carroll, chapter 4 · NIST CODATA constants

The predicted clock signal is about 1/20,500 of the statistical precision in Bothwell’s two-region comparison. That comparison gives a sense of scale. Choosing a detector for a movable source would require calculating its signal and uncertainty in the actual geometry and frequency band. Bothwell et al., Fig. 4

What would count as a tidal signal?

Imagine releasing two small probes side by side along the line toward the source. The closer one is pulled more strongly, so the probes begin to separate. With the baseline turned transverse to the radial direction, their accelerations have components toward one another. The direction and size of these differential signals give more information than a single acceleration reading. Carroll, chapter 3

In general relativity, this is described by geodesic deviation. For the torsion-free Levi-Civita connection in a coordinate basis, use the Riemann convention \([\nabla_\alpha,\nabla_\beta]V^\mu=R^\mu{}_{\nu\alpha\beta}V^\nu\). The relative acceleration along a reference free-fall trajectory is

\[ \frac{D^2\xi^\mu}{D\tau^2}=-R^\mu{}_{\nu\alpha\beta}u^\nu\xi^\alpha u^\beta. \]

Here \(\tau\) is proper time on the reference trajectory, \(u^\mu\) is its four-velocity, and \(\xi^\mu\) is an infinitesimal separation toward a neighbouring free-fall trajectory. In the reference probe’s freely falling orthonormal frame, with components measured with length-valued time coordinate \(x^0=ct\), so \(u^0=c\), the spatial tidal acceleration is \(-c^2R^i{}_{0j0}\xi^j\). A sensor with one orientation samples a projection of this response. A real gradiometer has a finite baseline, and its analysis must account for reference-frame motion and force gradients that can mimic tides. Carroll, chapter 3, Eqs. 3.67 and 3.113

How would we test a new device?

Start with a prediction for the size, sign, timing and spatial pattern of each measured signal. Calculate the ordinary gravitational contribution from anything that moves. Calibrate with a known signal and run controls that reproduce the switching, heating, vibration or electrical load as closely as possible. Use synchronized environmental measurements and document what remains uncertain. A sham also has mass, so its ordinary gravity belongs in the control model.

Imagine that the clock frequency shifts, an atom interferometer reports a phase change, and a mechanical sensor registers a force. A vibrating platform or a shared power supply could disturb all three. If a proposed source predicts both a clock-rate change and an acceleration gradient, ask whether one set of source parameters explains their sizes, signs and spatial patterns within the combined uncertainty, including shared errors.

Repeated trials, randomized source-state sequences and blinded analysis where practical can help test the result. Independent reproduction can add evidence. If the data support a quantitative bound, report the signal amplitudes constrained, the confidence level and the operating conditions. Preserve runs that gave inconclusive results, along with unexpected residuals and their uncertainties.

For Beyond the Light Barrier, the same care applies when comparing a supported Earth lab, a brief period of free fall, an orbiting platform and a weak-field environment far from Earth. In a supported lab, the floor supplies an upward force. In a drop test, the apparatus falls briefly. In orbit, the apparatus and its contents can fall together for much longer while Earth’s gravity and tidal curvature remain. Far from Earth, its contribution can be weaker while other bodies still contribute. A model must specify whether it depends on support acceleration, gravitational field strength in a specified frame, potential differences relevant to a clock comparison, the relative motion of free-fall probes or another observable. The supplied BTLB Research State v1.11 records no physical demonstration of a device that creates a novel spacetime geometry. The proposed tests here describe how evidence for a specified effect could be evaluated. Carroll, chapters 4 and 7 · BTLB Research Method overview

A useful test ends with a concrete account of what the device did in the conditions tested. The measured pattern may follow ordinary gravity, point to a disturbance in the apparatus, bound the size of a proposed effect or leave a residual for another experiment to investigate.

Evidence classification — Published experiments and observations illustrate established evidence (Category 1). The physical framework is accepted theory (Category 2). The 1,000 kg example is an analytic estimate (Category 6). The suggested tests are experimental considerations. This article presents no new BTLB physical result, simulation or adopted WC/WD model.

Sources and further reading

  • T. Bothwell et al., Nature 602, 420–424 (2022). Gravitational redshift within a strontium sample
  • M. Kasevich and S. Chu, Physical Review Letters 67, 181–184 (1991). Raman atom interferometry
  • J. B. Fixler et al., Science 315, 74–77 (2007). Atom-interferometric measurement of the Newtonian constant
  • A. Peters, K. Y. Chung and S. Chu, Nature 400, 849–852 (1999). Gravimetry using falling atoms
  • B. P. Abbott et al. (LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration), Physical Review Letters 116, 061102 (2016). Discovery of GW150914
  • S. M. Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity (1997). Curvature, gravitation and weak-field theory
